analysis.one_liner: Raises the base minimum wage for tipped workers from $2.13 toward 70% of the full minimum wage.
analysis.headline: The bill to raise tipped workers' base wage never got a committee vote and died when the 113th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under federal law, restaurants can pay tipped employees as little as $2.13 an hour in cash wages, with tips expected to bring them up to the $7.25 minimum. This bill would raise that base to $3.75 an hour, then $5.00, then 70% of the full federal minimum wage — at least $5.50 — with future adjustments tied to the regular minimum wage. It also required the Labor Department to publish notice before any increase. The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and never received a hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Roughly four million tipped workers — servers, bartenders, hairdressers, and others whose employers pay the $2.13 'tipped minimum wage' — would get a higher guaranteed cash wage that does not depend on tips. Workers whose tips fall short, including back-of-house and slow-shift workers, would be the clearest winners.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal base cash wage for tipped employees in steps: $3.75 an hour, then $5.00, then 70% of the full minimum wage (no less than $5.50), compared with the $2.13 in current law [S2][S3].

Requires the Department of Labor to publish notice in the Federal Register and online at least 10 days before any tipped-minimum increase takes effect, so employers and workers know the new rate [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Restaurant and hospitality employers would pay more in direct wages. Because tips make up the difference under current law, some employers might also see customers tip less or face pressure on menu prices; the industry argues the increase would cut jobs or hours for the same workers it aims to help.

drawbacks.text: The restaurant industry and many economists argue that raising the tipped base wage forces employers to cover more payroll and can lead to reduced hours, fewer staff, or lower tip income, offsetting part of the gain for the workers it targets (a general policy objection, not in the provided sources).

The bill raised only the base cash wage, not the full minimum wage, so even at $5.50 tipped workers would still earn well below the standard federal minimum before tips; a stronger alternative was to eliminate the tip credit entirely, which this bill did not do [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a moderate step: it did not abolish the two-tier tipped minimum wage, but it would have raised the floor under millions of low-paid workers and reduced workers' dependence on tips to reach the minimum. The main cost falls on employers in the restaurant sector, and the main uncertainty is how much of the wage increase would be offset by changes in tips, hours, or staffing. On balance it was a targeted wage floor with a real but partial benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The House committee it was assigned to never took it up, so it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Introduced February 13, 2013 by Rep. Donna Edwards with 20 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1][S3].
Referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce on the day of introduction [S5].

In April 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections, where it remained; it never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and no companion action is recorded in the House or Senate before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Restaurant and hospitality employers keep paying the $2.13 tipped base wage, and tipped workers got no raise. The committee majority that never scheduled the bill also avoided a recorded vote on the issue.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Restaurant employers; tipped workers got nothing

sides.party_line_note: The bill had 29 cosponsors, all Democrats, and no recorded vote ever occurred; its fate was decided in a committee controlled by the House Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would have required restaurants, bars, salons, and other tip-based businesses to pay a higher guaranteed cash wage instead of $2.13. Under the tip-credit system, employers rely on customer tips to cover most of their workers' base pay, so a higher floor directly raises their payroll costs.
Roughly a few million workers earn the sub-minimum tipped wage and depend on tips to reach $7.25; the bill would have guaranteed them a steadily higher base wage.
